name: First Vatican Council
also_known_as: Vatican I; twentieth ecumenical council (Catholic count)
summary: Pope Pius IX's council, which defined papal infallibility and the pope's universal jurisdiction, and was cut short when Italian troops took Rome.

end.label: Council suspended after Italian troops take Rome

background.text: Pius IX had lost most of the Papal States to the new Kingdom of Italy and had condemned modern errors in the Syllabus of Errors (1864). The ultramontane movement wanted papal authority strengthened.

happened.text: About 700 bishops attended. The constitution Dei Filius (24 April 1870) taught that God can be known with certainty by natural reason and that faith and reason cannot contradict each other.

The constitution Pastor Aeternus (18 July 1870) defined that the pope has full and immediate jurisdiction over the whole church, and that when he speaks ex cathedra to define a doctrine of faith or morals he is infallible, and such definitions are irreformable 'of themselves, and not from the consent of the church'.

About 60 bishops of the minority, who thought the definition unwise or untrue, left Rome the day before the final vote rather than vote against it before the pope. The vote was 533 to 2; the two bishops who voted no submitted immediately.
The Franco-Prussian War broke out the next day; French troops left Rome, Italian forces captured it on 20 September 1870, and Pius IX suspended the council indefinitely on 20 October.

participants.name: Henry Edward Manning
participants.role: Archbishop of Westminster; leader of the infallibilist majority

participants.name: Félix Dupanloup
participants.role: Bishop of Orléans; leader of the minority

participants.name: John Henry Newman
participants.role: Not present; thought the definition inopportune but accepted it, and defended it against Gladstone in 1875

participants.name: Ignaz von Döllinger
participants.role: Munich church historian who rejected the definition

outcomes.text: Papal infallibility has been invoked explicitly once since, for the Assumption of Mary (1950); Catholic theologians also count the 1854 Immaculate Conception.
Groups in Germany, Switzerland, and Austria who rejected the decrees formed the Old Catholic churches, joining the Union of Utrecht in 1889.
Protestant and Orthodox churches rejected the decrees, and they became a major issue in later ecumenical dialogue; the council's work on bishops was left unfinished until Vatican II.

condemnations.by: Archbishop Gregor von Scherr of Munich
condemnations.reason: Ignaz von Döllinger excommunicated for refusing to accept the decrees on infallibility
condemnations.status: Never lifted; he died in 1890 without reconciling, though he never joined the Old Catholics formally

condemnations.reason: Anathema on anyone who contradicts the definition of papal infallibility or universal jurisdiction
condemnations.status: In force in the Catholic Church

persecution_note: Opponents of the decrees were disciplined by the church, and in Germany the state turned on the Catholic Church partly in reaction to the council.

persecution.title: The Kulturkampf in Germany
persecution.summary: Otto von Bismarck's government, citing the danger of papal power after the council, passed laws expelling the Jesuits (1872) and, in the May Laws of 1873, putting the training and appointment of clergy under state control. Bishops and priests who refused were fined, imprisoned, or exiled; Archbishop Mieczysław Ledóchowski of Gniezno-Poznań was imprisoned in 1874.

responsible.name: Otto von Bismarck
responsible.role: Chancellor of Germany and Prussian minister-president

responsible.name: Adalbert Falk
responsible.role: Prussian minister of culture; author of the May Laws

persecution.outcome: Many dioceses and parishes left vacant; most laws were eased from 1878.

sources.citation: Norman P. Tanner (ed.), Decrees of the Ecumenical Councils, vol. 2. London: Sheed & Ward; Washington, DC: Georgetown University Press, 1990.
Cuthbert Butler, The Vatican Council 1869–1870, Based on Bishop Ullathorne's Letters. London: Longmans, Green, 1930.
John W. O'Malley, Vatican I: The Council and the Making of the Ultramontane Church. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 2018.

decisions: Dogmas: papal infallibility when speaking ex cathedra and the pope's universal jurisdiction (Pastor Aeternus); God knowable by reason (Dei Filius).
